titre_video: $40 Trillion Debt Passed. The American ECONOMY Is Collapsing

segments.titre: Washington lost the biggest gamble in financial history
segments.resume: Opening hook: for over a decade US policymakers financed the country with ultra-cheap short-term debt, betting near-zero interest rates would last forever. That bet has now been lost.
segments.texte: Washington just lost the biggest gamble in financial history. For over a decade, policymakers have run America on ultra cheap, short term debt betting that near zero interest rates would last forever. That bet just lost.

segments.titre: Annual interest passes $1.25 trillion, above defense spending
segments.resume: For the first time, America's annual interest bill crossed $1.25 trillion and surpassed the national defense budget. Taxpayer money goes to past borrowing before it can fund roads, schools or hospitals, and ordinary Americans foot the bill.
segments.texte: For the first time ever, America’s annual interest crossed $1.25 trillion, officially eclipsing the national defense budget. Taxpayer money was sucked into past borrowing before a penny can be spent repairing roads, upgrading schools or building hospitals. It’s not a future crisis. It’s already here… and DC isn’t picking up the tab. You are.

segments.titre: $970 billion of interest and $2,800 per American
segments.resume: In the 2025 budget year Washington spent $970 billion on interest alone, none of it improving the country. This equals about $2,800 per American, and nearly a fifth of federal revenue goes straight to bondholders, foreign nations and hedge funds.
segments.texte: Across the 2025 budget year, Washington burned through $970 billion in interest alone. Not a single dollar went to improving the country. Instead, it was covering loans taken out years ago. That works out to $2,800 taken away from every single American. You didn’t vote for these charges. You didn’t agree to them. But your employer withheld them from your paycheck before you even saw a dime. Today, nearly a fifth of everything the government collects is immediately handed over to bondholders, foreign nations and Wall Street hedge funds.

segments.titre: A dollar of interest buys nothing
segments.resume: Compares a dollar spent on defense or Medicaid, which buys a warship or a hospital visit, with a dollar spent on interest, which buys absolutely nothing. Americans pay the price of years of reckless spending.
segments.texte: A dollar spent on defense helps fund a warship. A dollar funneled into Medicaid helps provide a hospital visit. A dollar spent on interest buys absolutely nothing. Americans are paying the price for years of reckless spending.

segments.titre: The financial doom loop
segments.resume: The US is borrowing new money just to pay interest on its old money, a doom loop. Interest on the debt was $476 billion in 2022 and has more than doubled in three years.
segments.texte: The country is in a financial doom loop. The U.S. is officially borrowing new money just to pay off the interest on its old money. In 2022, the interest on the debt was $476 billion. In just 3 years, it has more than doubled.

segments.titre: How the Treasury's short-term borrowing was engineered
segments.resume: The Treasury can lock in 30-year bonds like a fixed-rate mortgage or gamble on short-term paper. It rolled debt over at very low rates for years, but the clock ran out and trillions must now be refinanced at crippling rates after the 2022 rate spike.
segments.texte: But this economic disaster didn’t happen by accident. It was engineered. Every time the Treasury borrows, a clock starts ticking. They can lock in a 30-year bond, just like a fixed rate mortgage. Or they can take a risk on short paper, loans that are due in a few months or years. For years, the Treasury rolled debt over at shockingly low rates, treating it like free cash. It seemed like a good idea at the time. By picking the low rate option, they saved billion. But now, that ticking clock just ran out. And the Treasury is forced to renegotiate those trillions of dollars at today’s crippling rates. 2022 was a brutal year for borrowers but it was unprecedented for the government. The interest rates they used to rely on skyrocketed and lenders demanded their money right away. The government only survived by doubling down. The country's debt burden was already heavy. The debt repricing only made it worse.

segments.titre: July 2026 deficit and spending beyond means
segments.resume: Even with a strong economy and low unemployment, the government kept spending beyond its means. In July 2026 it had its fourth worst spending month in history, spending $432 billion more than it raised.
segments.texte: Normally this kind of crisis happens during a war or a devastating recession. But the economy at the time was strong and unemployment low. But the government was still spending beyond its means. It all reached a breaking point in July 2026. The government faced the fourth worst spending month in American history, spending $432 billion more than it raised. Debt is being piled on top of debt. Now it’s catching up on them.

segments.titre: Interest share of tax receipts nearly doubled
segments.resume: Cutting government programs would not fix it because interest is the problem. Interest rose from 8.7% of tax receipts in 2021 to 18.5% by end of 2025, the highest since the early 1990s, but now the cause is the huge debt burden rather than high rates.
segments.texte: It’s easy to blame public spending for all of this. But freezing government programs wouldn’t actually help. The interest is the problem. Interest spending was 8.7% of total tax receipts in 2021. By the end of 2025, it had nearly doubled to 18.5%. That’s the highest it’s been since the early 90s. But back then, the debt burden was low, even though interest rates were high. Today, it’s the opposite. Rates are low, but the monumental debt burden makes things more expensive.

segments.titre: Interest as share of GDP and a quarter of revenue
segments.resume: Interest takes 3.3% of GDP and is on track for 4.6% by 2036. Excluding the Social Security payroll tax, it swallows a quarter of remaining revenue, like a household earning $60,000 with a $12,000 credit card interest bill.
segments.texte: Right now, interest eats up 3.3% of the country's GDP. According to the current trajectory, it will be at 4.6% by 2036. It’s even worse than it seems. A large part of federal revenue is the payroll tax, devoted to Social Security. After removing that, interest effectively swallows a quarter of the remaining revenue. It’s like a household bringing in $60,000 in a year. Before any money is spent on groceries, there’s a $12,000 bill for credit card interest. No one would consider that to be a financially stable household.

segments.titre: The maturity wall: $9.7 trillion due
segments.resume: About a third of the debt owed to the public, roughly $9.7 trillion, comes due by end of 2027 and the Treasury needs buyers for all of it. Refinancing is dictated by the timeline, so the average rate keeps rising regardless of the Fed.
segments.texte: About a third of what the Treasury owes to the public is due by the end of 2027. That comes to roughly $9.7 trillion that has to be paid back this year. And the Treasury desperately has to find a buyer for all of it. Washington doesn’t have the luxury of picking and choosing when to refinance. It’s dictated by the timeline, no matter how bad interest rates are. As a result, the average rate the government pays continues to increase, despite what the Fed does. Each time they sell off bonds, they’re getting higher and higher rates. That money has to come from somewhere.

segments.titre: Interest crowds out public spending
segments.resume: Interest payments outpace a roughly $112 billion annual spending category by about 9 to 1, with school districts, public lands and national parks affected. Infrastructure is swallowed by a financial black hole, and programs are dropped quietly without being called cuts.
segments.texte: Each year around $112 billion is spent by the federal government. Interest payments outpace that by roughly 9 to 1. School districts are feeling the effects before Washington does. Public lands and national parks are being outpaced by an even greater margin. America’s infrastructure is being swallowed by a financial black hole. It’s voracious. None of this gets called a cut. Programs are just dropped and nobody has to give an explanation.

segments.titre: Treasury yields raise borrowing costs for everyone
segments.resume: Treasury yields set the floor for mortgages, car loans and credit cards. In August 2026 the 30-year yield hit 5.31% and a 30-year auction priced at 5.21%, the steepest since 2001; a quarter point on a $350,000 loan costs about $660 a year.
segments.texte: But the government's own books aren't the only ones feeling the squeeze. Treasury yields set the floor for nearly every loan in the U.S. Mortgages, car loans, and credit card debts all sit on it. In August 2026, the 30 year treasury yield hit 5.31%. At the same time, the government was selling 30-year bonds with a yield of 5.21%, the steepest yield at any auction since 2001. That shows up in mortgage and loan payments for ordinary Americans. Just a quarter point on a $350,000 loan is about $55 a month. That's $660 a year, and it sounds survivable until you realize it came from borrowing decisions over a decade ago. When Washington borrows more, so does the rest of the country. The government uses your money to pay interest and raises the cost of your own debt in the process.

segments.titre: Global demand for Treasuries is cracking
segments.resume: For 80 years dollar demand made Treasuries the safest place for cash, with central banks buying trillions; Japan holds about $1.1 trillion. That global loyalty is cracking as buyers at weekly auctions say no thanks.
segments.texte: For 80 years, this was never an issue. All over the world, there was a demand for dollars, and the safest place to park cash was a U.S. Treasury bond. Central banks would buy U.S. Treasury bonds in the trillions without ever worrying about the price. Even now, Tokyo's government holds about $1.1 trillion of these bonds, making them a load-bearing part of your tax bill. But that global loyalty is cracking. The auctions happen every week. Only a few banks are required to make a bid. Every other potential buyer in the world has to decide if the yield is worth the risk. And lately those global buyers are saying “no thanks.”

segments.titre: Tails and the failed August 2026 20-year auction
segments.resume: A tail means a bond sale went badly and the government must offer higher rates, which taxpayers pay for 30 years. In August 2026 a $16 billion 20-year auction saw weak demand and dealers of last resort took 12.5% of the sale.
segments.texte: When a bond sale doesn't go well, traders call it a "tail." It’s a polite way of saying it’s a disaster. It means buyers didn’t turn up, so the government had to sweeten the deal by offering higher interest rates just to get the money. And it’s the taxpayers who have to pay off those sweetened, high interest rates for the next 30 years. In August 2026, the Treasury tried to sell off $16 billion of 20-year bonds. To say demand was low is being kind. The preferred buyers were turning their backs on the bonds. So it was left to the banks of last resort, the dealers required to bid, snapping up 12.5% of the sale, well above the normal amounts. The free market was running away. And alarm bells were ringing in Washington.

segments.titre: Treasury buys back its own debt
segments.resume: On August 19th Treasury doubled its buyback operations from $2 billion to $4 billion, and Secretary Bessent said it would make a market for its own debt. The department used its own cash to prop up the market after long yields hit a 19-year high.
segments.texte: On August 19th, the Treasury Department announced that it would at least double the size of its buyback operations, increasing them from $2 billion to $4 billion. The next day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent appeared on television and said that his department would make a market for its own debt. The government department tasked with auctioning off bonds admitted no one wanted to buy the bonds. So, they’re using their own cash to buy their own debt… just to prop up the market. They changed this rule pretty quickly, just days after long yields reached a 19-year high.

segments.titre: Investors try to dump $95 billion of long bonds
segments.resume: Investors offered $95 billion of long bonds to a buyback program capped at $8 billion, and $50 billion of 10-20 year bonds for a $6 billion limit. The limits were the only thing stopping more bonds being unloaded.
segments.texte: Sellers were panicking, already waiting to unload American debt. Investors tried to dump $95 billion of long bonds onto a government program with a limit of $8 billion. The government bought what it could, but had to reject the rest. That leaves a lot of people trying to get rid of the bonds they don’t want. And that the taxpayers are servicing. The same thing happened with the shorter end of the bond. Investors offered $50 billion of 10-20 year bonds for operations with a limit of $6 billion. Once again, the limit was the only thing that stopped more bonds being unloaded.

segments.titre: Buybacks funded by short-term debt, and the price of reserve status
segments.resume: To fund buybacks of long bonds the Treasury sells short-term loans, repeating the original mistake. A $4 billion buyback is tiny against $31.4 trillion of marketable debt, but trying it signals market rejection; the dollar's reserve status remains but the world charges more for it.
segments.texte: The Treasury can’t print money out of thin air to buy back the long term bonds. To get the cash, they have to sell the short term loans over the space of a few months. Sound familiar? It’s the same situation that started this crisis in the first place. Washington is pouring gasoline on the fire, just because the payments look smaller at this time. Of course, a $4 billion buy back is nothing compared to the $31.4 trillion of marketable debt. It’s barely a tenth of a percent of what is outstanding. Anyone claiming that the bond market broke in August 2026 is trying to sell you something. What is important is that the government tried it at all. These emergency debt buy backs started in 2024 as a behind the scenes technical tool. But they were run multiple times throughout 2025. By the end of the year, the operation had more than doubled in size. You don’t take that kind of risk unless the market is actively rejecting you. The privilege of being the world’s reserve currency hasn’t been taken away from America. It’s just that the world is charging the U.S. more to keep it that way.

segments.titre: Why the Fed can't just cut rates
segments.resume: The Fed is constrained: rates held at 3.5 to 3.75% for five meetings, with three members voting to raise at the last one and inflation at 3.5% in June 2026 versus a 2% target. Even a cut would give less relief than people expect.
segments.texte: This is where the most obvious answer comes in, and it is the answer that every comment section arrives at. So why doesn’t the Fed just cut rates? First, the Federal Reserve is operating with handcuffs on. They have kept rates at 3.5 to 3.75% for 5 consecutive meetings. During the last meeting, 3 of their own members voted to increase rates. Inflation was still 3.5% in June 2026, which was well above the Federal Reserve's safe target of 2%.. Even if the Fed caved and slashed rates, the relief would be less than people think. It wouldn’t save the nation.

segments.titre: Rate cuts don't fix existing debt
segments.resume: Cutting the Fed's rate does not change contracts or bonds already sold, nor shrink the $32 trillion held by the public. If cuts come from a stalling economy, tax revenue falls and interest cost as a share of revenue gets worse.
segments.texte: Lowering the Fed's daily interest rate doesn’t affect the contracts or bonds that have already been sold. It doesn’t shrink the $32 trillion in bonds that the public already holds. If the Fed cuts because the economy is stalling, your paycheck shrinks along with the government’s tax revenue. While the dollar cost of debt service may decrease, the share of interest cost to the government actually worsens.

segments.titre: Fiscal dominance and the WWII precedent
segments.resume: If the Fed cut rates purely to bail out the Treasury, lenders would demand higher rates, making refinancing harder. This is fiscal dominance, which happened during and after World War II when bonds were repaid but inflation wiped out their value.
segments.texte: But what if the Fed cuts rates purely to bail out the Treasury? Lenders all over the world will notice immediately. They’ll realize that the government is willing to sacrifice the dollar just to keep its head above water. To protect themselves, lenders would demand even higher rates before buying any more American bonds. Long term rates will keep rising, and refinancing the country’s debt will be even harder. It’s a scenario known as fiscal dominance. It’s when a government's runaway budget comes before everything else, including the ability to keep prices stable. It’s happened in the United States before. During and after the Second World War, the Federal Reserve lowered interest rates to help the Treasury. Bonds didn't default, but their value was completely wiped out because of inflation. Anyone who bought a war bond got their money, but those dollars covered a small fraction of what the bond was worth.

segments.titre: Two options: higher rates or a weaker dollar
segments.resume: The government can accept higher rates and let the budget be cannibalized, or let the currency lose value and repay with cheaper dollars. The first eats public services, the second eats personal savings.
segments.texte: The government is faced with two options. The first is accept the higher rates and watch the budget get cannibalized. Or let the currency lose value and use the hyper inflated, cheaper dollars to settle the debt. The first option eats into public services. The second option eats into your personal savings.

segments.titre: No default, but a slow erosion
segments.resume: America will not default because it borrows in a currency it creates and will pay on time and in full. That is why the risk is dangerous: no dramatic collapse, but interest keeps growing, room for everything else shrinks and money buys less each year.
segments.texte: None of this means America is about to default on its debt. And that’s important. The United States borrows in a currency it creates out of thin air. It will make every single payment, on time and in full. And it will continue to do so for a long time. And that’s why the risk is so dangerous. A country that is always able to print more money will never experience a dramatic, Hollywood style economic collapse. Interest will keep growing, and the room for everything else will keep shrinking. The money in your account will buy less every year. And it’s already happening.

segments.titre: Everyday effects: inflation erodes savings
segments.resume: Groceries, rent and mortgages cost more while raises shrink, in small incremental changes. Losing 3% of value yearly means $10,000 saved is worth about $7,400 in a decade, though the statement still shows $10,000.
segments.texte: Your grocery bill increases by a few percent. Your rent or your mortgage payment increases. Your boss gives you a smaller raise… or none at all. It’s small, incremental changes. But over the course of a decade, the impact hits home. Losing 3% of your value each year means that every $10,000 saved is only worth around $7,400. Your statement will still show it is worth $10,000. But your spending power is weaker.

segments.titre: CBO projections for interest costs
segments.resume: The CBO expects interest to reach almost $2.1 trillion by 2036, over a quarter of revenue, and 37% of revenue by the 2050s. America will pay $16.2 trillion in interest over the next decade, close to double the previous two decades combined.
segments.texte: By 2036, the Congressional Budget Office, or CBO, expects interest to reach almost $2.1 trillion. Measured against revenue, that's over a quarter of everything the government brings in. By the 2050s, under current policies, interest payments will consume 37% of all the money the government takes in. Over the next decade, America will pay $16.2 trillion in interest. That's close to double what the country spent on interest across the previous two decades combined, even after adjusting for inflation. The problem is spiraling out of control. And no one can stop it.

segments.titre: A 1% rate rise and the per-person debt burden
segments.resume: Forecasts assume low rates; a 1% rise in average rates would add hundreds of billions yearly, like funding a second military budget for nothing. The debt costs about $117,000 per person and $297,000 per household.
segments.texte: All those forecasts rely on the belief that interest rates will stay low. Even just a small 1% increase in the average interest rate would instantly add hundreds of billions of dollars in extra costs each year. That’s the equivalent of funding an entire second U.S. military budget, covering it with taxes… and getting no protection or benefit in return. It now costs around $117,000 per person in the U.S. to pay off the national debt. That means the average household owes $297,000. That's what an extended period of cheap money has bought us. A bill landing on the doorstep of every single American.

segments.titre: How cheap money left a long-term liability
segments.resume: Washington used low rates to borrow massively and chose short-term notes because payments looked small, locking in a liability refinanced daily at market rates. Interest is now the third largest federal expense and is paid before anything else.
segments.texte: Washington took advantage of historically low interest rates to borrow massive amounts of money. It opted to pay the short-term notes because the principal and interest payments seemed small. The government has locked in a long-term liability, committing to refinance it on a secondary market that resets every day and charges whatever the market determines. Interest is now the third largest thing the federal government does with money, ahead of every other agency and every program. Interest payments are made before any other payments are made, and the amount that is withheld from your pay regardless if the economy is strong or weak.

segments.titre: Washington gambled and lost; the debt is called in
segments.resume: Closing statement that Washington gambled with America's money and lost, and the debt is now being called in.
segments.texte: Washington gambled with America's money… and lost. And now the debt is being called in.

segments.titre: Call to action: watch what if the US economy crashes
segments.resume: The speaker says the debt is out of control and threatens millions of livelihoods, and points viewers to another video about the fallout if the US economy crashes.
segments.texte: The U.S. debt is out of control and it’s threatening the livelihood of millions. But what if the worst actually happened? Watch “What If The US Economy CRASHES” to see how the fallout would affect you. Or click on this.
